<reason>PRO built a competent, disciplined case (free curbs still ration via queues; time limits don't resolve simultaneous demand; pricing shifts flexible trips before the jam) and handled the "that isn't dynamic" semantic attack well. But CON progressively narrowed the debate to a single contested component—"my model plus a fee"—and made the fee justify itself alone. CON's sharpest moves were showing that off-hour incentives work because they pay the receiver who controls the window while a curb fee lands on the courier who doesn't, and then leveraging PRO's own honest concessions ("that courier may change nothing"; "the charge has not managed demand") into a coherent story that the fee taxes the party without the lever, displaces rather than reduces demand, and sorts by balance sheet. PRO's florist counter (one immobilized van vs. a fleet absorbing delay) was its best live route and CON's "exit dressed as efficiency" answer is more assertion than proof, but PRO never fully rebuilt the affirmative behavioral story after the concessions. CON's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a real execution cost and its "inelastic core" premise was overclaimed, which keeps this competitive rather than a solid win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B2.3–B2.8: CON's reply that off-hour programs pay the receiver (the decision-maker) while a curb fee hits the courier, plus "pricing does not conjure a second bay—it decides who gets the first one," reframed PRO's shared tools as CON's and isolated the fee as the only contested, cost-adding element; PRO never fully recovered the mechanism story after this.</best_rebuttal>
